# 17 — Algebraic Graph Methods and Polynomial Randomization

Determinants encode signed cycle covers.  Choosing the matrix entries carefully
makes unwanted covers cancel, leaving spanning trees, matchings, or parity
structures.  Random evaluation then turns a symbolic nonzeroness question into
finite-field linear algebra.

## 1. Pfaffians and hafnians

For an even-dimensional skew-symmetric matrix $A$, the Pfaffian sums signed
products over perfect pairings and satisfies

$$\operatorname{Pf}(A)^{2}=\det A.$$

Eliminate pairs of rows/columns together.  If pivot `A[i][j]` is used, swap
indices into the active pair, account for the Pfaffian sign, multiply the pivot,
and apply the skew-symmetric Schur-complement update.  This is $O(n^{3})$ over a
field of characteristic not two.  The hafnian removes signs and directly counts
weighted perfect pairings, but its general algorithms are exponential.

## 2. Tutte matrix

For an undirected graph, put an indeterminate $x_ij$ above the diagonal,
$-x_ij$ below it, and zero on nonedges.  Its determinant is a nonzero polynomial
iff the graph has a perfect matching.  Substituting independent random field
values yields a one-sided-error $O(n^{3})$ test.  With high probability, the
matrix rank is twice the maximum matching size.

## 3. Schwartz–Zippel and PIT

A nonzero polynomial of total degree $d$ evaluated uniformly over a finite set
$S$ vanishes with probability at most $d/|S|$.  Record all three quantities:
degree, field size, and number of trials.  Random evaluation can produce a false
zero but never a false symbolic witness.  Use fresh randomness, avoid tiny
fields, and repeat when the error budget is not negligible.

## 4. Determinant polynomials and updates

$det(A+xB)$ packages a family of rank/determinant questions into one polynomial;
evaluate at enough field points and interpolate.  The matrix determinant lemma
and Sherman–Morrison give rank-one updates when the required inverse exists.
The adjugate identity

$$A\operatorname{adj}(A)=\det(A)I$$

remains meaningful when $A$ is singular and is often the safer symbolic object.
